1. # Evaluators catalog
2. 
3. Full catalog of evaluators wired by `setup-maf-evals`, grouped by tier.
4. The skill defaults to Tier 1 (NLP) always on, Tier 2 (Quality) on but
5. gated by `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE`, Tier 3 (Safety) off unless opted in.
6. 
7. Source: [learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/ai/evaluation/libraries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/ai/evaluation/libraries)
8. 
9. ## Tier 1 — NLP (deterministic, no LLM)
10. 
11. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Evaluation.NLP` (preview — added via `--prerelease`).
12. 
13. | Evaluator | Metric | Context type needed | Notes |
14. |-----------|--------|---------------------|-------|
15. | `BLEUEvaluator` | `BLEU` | `BLEUEvaluatorContext(IEnumerable<string> references)` | n-gram overlap with one or more reference strings |
16. | `GLEUEvaluator` | `GLEU` | `GLEUEvaluatorContext(IEnumerable<string> references)` | sentence-level BLEU variant |
17. | `F1Evaluator` | `F1` | `F1EvaluatorContext(string groundTruth)` | unigram-level F1 |
18. 
19. Plus a built-in custom evaluator the skill always scaffolds:
20. 
21. | Evaluator | Metric | Why |
22. |-----------|--------|-----|
23. | `WordCountEvaluator` (custom) | `Words` | Sanity check: response is non-empty and reasonable length. Same pattern as the Learn doc tutorial. |
24. 
25. ### `WordCountEvaluator` reference implementation
26. 
27. Scaffold this file verbatim (the Learn-doc canonical pattern) into
28. `Reporting/WordCountEvaluator.cs`. It runs in stub tier with no API key.
29. 
30. ```csharp
31. public sealed class WordCountEvaluator : IEvaluator
32. {
33.     public const string MetricName = "Words";
34.     public IReadOnlyCollection<string> EvaluationMetricNames { get; } = [MetricName];
35. 
36.     public ValueTask<EvaluationResult> EvaluateAsync(
37.         IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
38.         ChatResponse modelResponse,
39.         ChatConfiguration? chatConfiguration = null,
40.         IEnumerable<EvaluationContext>? additionalContext = null,
41.         CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
42.     {
43.         var text = modelResponse?.Text ?? string.Empty;
44.         var count = text.Split(
45.             new[] { ' ', '\t', '\r', '\n' },
46.             StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length;
47. 
48.         var metric = new NumericMetric(MetricName, value: count)
49.         {
50.             Interpretation = count switch
51.             {
52.                 < 5   => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Poor,    reason: "Response too short"),
53.                 > 500 => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Average, reason: "Response very long"),
54.                 _     => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Good),
55.             }
56.         };
57.         return new ValueTask<EvaluationResult>(new EvaluationResult(metric));
58.     }
59. }
60. ```
61. 
62. ## Tier 2 — Quality (LLM-as-judge)
63. 
64. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Evaluation.Quality` (GA — latest stable).
65. 
66. Requires `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE=1` and a real `IChatClient`. The skill
67. wires the following by default:
68. 
69. | Evaluator | Metric | Context type | Notes |
70. |-----------|--------|--------------|-------|
71. | `RelevanceEvaluator` | `Relevance` | none | how relevant is the response to the query |
72. | `CoherenceEvaluator` | `Coherence` | none | logical, orderly presentation |
73. | `FluencyEvaluator` | `Fluency` | none | grammar, readability |
74. | `CompletenessEvaluator` | `Completeness` | `CompletenessEvaluatorContext(string groundTruth)` | comprehensive and accurate |
75. | `EquivalenceEvaluator` | `Equivalence` | `EquivalenceEvaluatorContext(string groundTruth)` | similarity vs ground truth wrt query |
76. | `GroundednessEvaluator` | `Groundedness` | `GroundednessEvaluatorContext(string context)` | alignment with given context |
77. 
78. Agent-focused (added when `*.AppHost.csproj` is detected, indicating
79. this is an agentic app and not just a chat completion app):
80. 
81. | Evaluator | Metric | Context type | Notes |
82. |-----------|--------|--------------|-------|
83. | `IntentResolutionEvaluator` | `Intent Resolution` | none | identifies + resolves user intent |
84. | `TaskAdherenceEvaluator` | `Task Adherence` | none | sticks to assigned task |
85. | `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluator` | `Tool Call Accuracy` | `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluatorContext(...)` | uses tools correctly |
86. 
87. **Not wired by default:** `RelevanceTruthAndCompletenessEvaluator`
88. (marked experimental in upstream docs), `RetrievalEvaluator` (specific
89. to RAG pipelines — separate skill territory).
90. 
91. ## Tier 3 — Safety (Foundry Evaluation service)
92. 
93. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Evaluation.Safety` (preview — added via `--prerelease`).
94. 
95. Off by default. Enabled when user opts in during step 2 of the
96. workflow. Requires `EVAL_USE_FOUNDRY_SAFETY=1` and an Azure AI Foundry
97. endpoint (the skill prompts for `AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT` + Entra credentials).
98. 
99. **Always wire the bundle, not the 4 separate evaluators:**
100. 
101. | Evaluator | Metrics produced | Notes |
102. |-----------|------------------|-------|
103. | `ContentHarmEvaluator` | `Hate And Unfairness`, `Self Harm`, `Violence`, `Sexual` | **Single-shot — one Foundry call returns all 4 metrics.** Always prefer this over the 4 separate evaluators below. |
104. 
105. Additional safety evaluators (each wired as separate `[TestMethod]`):
106. 
107. | Evaluator | Metric | Notes |
108. |-----------|--------|-------|
109. | `ProtectedMaterialEvaluator` | `Protected Material` | copyrighted material in output |
110. | `IndirectAttackEvaluator` | `Indirect Attack` | prompt-injection-style indirect attacks |
111. | `CodeVulnerabilityEvaluator` | `Code Vulnerability` | vulnerable code in output |
112. | `UngroundedAttributesEvaluator` | `Ungrounded Attributes` | inferred human attributes |
113. | `GroundednessProEvaluator` | `Groundedness Pro` | fine-tuned Foundry-hosted groundedness check |
114. 
115. The 4 separate evaluators (`HateAndUnfairnessEvaluator`,
116. `SelfHarmEvaluator`, `ViolenceEvaluator`, `SexualEvaluator`) are
117. **not** scaffolded — they're a strict subset of `ContentHarmEvaluator`
118. and cost 4× more Foundry calls for the same metrics.
119. 
120. ## Threshold mapping
121. 
122. `quality.thresholds.json` maps **real MEAI metric names** to minimum
123. `EvaluationRating` enum values:
124. 
125. ```json
126. {
127.   "schema_version": 2,
128.   "hard_fail": false,
129.   "thresholds": {
130.     "Relevance":   { "min_rating": "Good" },
131.     "Coherence":   { "min_rating": "Good" },
132.     "Fluency":     { "min_rating": "Average" },
133.     "Groundedness":{ "min_rating": "Good" },
134.     "BLEU":        { "min_value": 0.20 },
135.     "F1":          { "min_value": 0.30 },
136.     "Words":       { "min_value": 5, "max_value": 500 }
137.   }
138. }
139. ```
140. 
141. `hard_fail: true` makes any below-threshold metric fail the test.
142. Default `false` makes the test pass-through informational — failures
143. show in the report only.
144. 
145. ## Custom rubric-driven evaluator
146. 
147. The built-in Quality evaluators (Relevance, Coherence, Fluency,
148. Completeness, Equivalence) judge against generic rubrics baked into
149. the evaluator's judge prompt. They cannot read `Quality/rubric.md`.
150. That makes them ill-fitting for agents with deliberate stylistic
151. constraints (ELI5 / summarizer / strict-format / persona-bound
152. agents) — see `common-pitfalls.md#tuning-quality-for-stylistic-agents`.
153. 
154. For those agents, scaffold a `RubricEvaluator` that reads
155. `Quality/rubric.md` and asks the judge to score against *your*
156. criteria. The pattern is shape-identical to `WordCountEvaluator` —
157. it just delegates to the judge chat client.
158. 
159. ```csharp
160. // Reporting/RubricEvaluator.cs
161. // Custom rubric-driven evaluator. Reads Quality/rubric.md and asks
162. // the judge to score the response against per-app criteria. Emits a
163. // single "RubricFit" metric (numeric 1-5) plus a free-text rationale.
164. public sealed class RubricEvaluator : IEvaluator
165. {
166.     public const string MetricName = "RubricFit";
167.     public IReadOnlyCollection<string> EvaluationMetricNames { get; } = [MetricName];
168. 
169.     private readonly string _rubric;
170. 
171.     public RubricEvaluator(string rubricMarkdown) => _rubric = rubricMarkdown;
172. 
173.     public static RubricEvaluator FromFile(string path) =>
174.         new(File.ReadAllText(path));
175. 
176.     public async ValueTask<EvaluationResult> EvaluateAsync(
177.         IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
178.         ChatResponse modelResponse,
179.         ChatConfiguration? chatConfiguration = null,
180.         IEnumerable<EvaluationContext>? additionalContext = null,
181.         CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
182.     {
183.         if (chatConfiguration?.ChatClient is null)
184.         {
185.             // Judge tier not active — return a stubbed Inconclusive metric.
186.             return new EvaluationResult(new NumericMetric(MetricName)
187.             {
188.                 Interpretation = new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(
189.                     EvaluationRating.Inconclusive, reason: "Judge not wired.")
190.             });
191.         }
192. 
193.         var userQuery = string.Join("\n", messages.Select(m => m.Text));
194.         var responseText = modelResponse.Text ?? string.Empty;
195. 
196.         // NOTE: $$"""...""" (double-$) raw string. Inside, single { } is literal
197.         // (matters for the JSON braces below), and {{var}} is interpolation.
198.         // Plain $"""...""" would reject `{{ ... }}` as literal with CS9006.
199.         var prompt = $$"""
200.             You are scoring an assistant response against the rubric below.
201. 
202.             ## Rubric
203.             {{_rubric}}
204. 
205.             ## User query
206.             {{userQuery}}
207. 
208.             ## Assistant response
209.             {{responseText}}
210. 
211.             Respond with strict JSON: { "score": <1-5 int>, "rationale": "<1-2 sentences>" }.
212.             5 = perfectly satisfies every rubric clause. 1 = ignores the rubric.
213.             """;
214. 
215.         var judge = await chatConfiguration.ChatClient.GetResponseAsync(
216.             prompt, cancellationToken: cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
217. 
218.         // Tolerant parse: fall back to Inconclusive on bad JSON.
219.         var (score, rationale) = TryParse(judge.Text ?? "");
220. 
221.         var metric = new NumericMetric(MetricName, value: score)
222.         {
223.             Interpretation = new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(
224.                 rating: score switch { >= 4 => EvaluationRating.Good,
225.                                        3    => EvaluationRating.Average,
226.                                        _    => EvaluationRating.Poor },
227.                 reason: rationale)
228.         };
229.         return new EvaluationResult(metric);
230.     }
231. 
232.     private static (int score, string rationale) TryParse(string raw)
233.     {
234.         try
235.         {
236.             using var doc = JsonDocument.Parse(raw.Trim().Trim('`', ' ', '\n', '\r'));
237.             return (doc.RootElement.GetProperty("score").GetInt32(),
238.                     doc.RootElement.GetProperty("rationale").GetString() ?? "");
239.         }
240.         catch { return (3, "Judge response was unparseable; defaulted to Average."); }
241.     }
242. }
243. ```
244. 
245. Wire it from `Reporting/ReportingConfig.cs`'s judge-tier evaluator
246. list **alongside** Relevance/Coherence/Fluency (drop Completeness +
247. Equivalence per the pitfall guidance):
248. 
249. ```csharp
250. // In ReportingConfig.ForQuality(), when EvalEnv.UseRealJudge:
251. evaluators.Add(new RelevanceEvaluator());
252. evaluators.Add(new CoherenceEvaluator());
253. evaluators.Add(new FluencyEvaluator());
254. evaluators.Add(RubricEvaluator.FromFile(
255.     Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "Quality", "rubric.md")));
256. // CompletenessEvaluator + EquivalenceEvaluator deliberately dropped
257. // for this app — see common-pitfalls.md tuning section.
258. ```
259. 
260. Ensure `Quality/rubric.md` is copied to output by adding to the csproj:
261. 
262. ```xml
263. <ItemGroup>
264.   <None Update="Quality/rubric.md" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
265. </ItemGroup>
266. ```
267. 
268. This `RubricFit` metric will appear in `report.html` alongside the
269. built-ins, and the rationale shows in the per-scenario detail drawer.
270. Update `Reporting/MetricsGlossary.cs`'s `QualityEntries` constant to
271. add a one-line `RubricFit` definition pointing at `Quality/rubric.md`.
272.

52.                 < 5   => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Poor,    reason: "Response too short"),
53.                 > 500 => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Average, reason: "Response very long"),
54.                 _     => new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(EvaluationRating.Good),
55.             }
56.         };
57.         return new ValueTask<EvaluationResult>(new EvaluationResult(metric));
58.     }
59. }
60. ```
61. 
62. ## Tier 2 — Quality (LLM-as-judge)
63. 
64. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Evaluation.Quality` (GA — latest stable).
65. 
66. Requires `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE=1` and a real `IChatClient`. The skill
67. wires the following by default:
68. 
69. | Evaluator | Metric | Context type | Notes |
70. |-----------|--------|--------------|-------|
71. | `RelevanceEvaluator` | `Relevance` | none | how relevant is the response to the query |
72. | `CoherenceEvaluator` | `Coherence` | none | logical, orderly presentation |
73. | `FluencyEvaluator` | `Fluency` | none | grammar, readability |
74. | `CompletenessEvaluator` | `Completeness` | `CompletenessEvaluatorContext(string groundTruth)` | comprehensive and accurate |
75. | `EquivalenceEvaluator` | `Equivalence` | `EquivalenceEvaluatorContext(string groundTruth)` | similarity vs ground truth wrt query |
76. | `GroundednessEvaluator` | `Groundedness` | `GroundednessEvaluatorContext(string context)` | alignment with given context |
77. 
78. Agent-focused (added when `*.AppHost.csproj` is detected, indicating
79. this is an agentic app and not just a chat completion app):
80. 
81. | Evaluator | Metric | Context type | Notes |
82. |-----------|--------|--------------|-------|
83. | `IntentResolutionEvaluator` | `Intent Resolution` | none | identifies + resolves user intent |
84. | `TaskAdherenceEvaluator` | `Task Adherence` | none | sticks to assigned task |
85. | `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluator` | `Tool Call Accuracy` | `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluatorContext(...)` | uses tools correctly |
86. 
87. **Not wired by default:** `RelevanceTruthAndCompletenessEvaluator`
88. (marked experimental in upstream docs), `RetrievalEvaluator` (specific
89. to RAG pipelines — separate skill territory).
90. 
91. ## Tier 3 — Safety (Foundry Evaluation service)
92. 
93. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Evaluation.Safety` (preview — added via `--prerelease`).
94. 
95. Off by default. Enabled when user opts in during step 2 of the
96. workflow. Requires `EVAL_USE_FOUNDRY_SAFETY=1` and an Azure AI Foundry
97. endpoint (the skill prompts for `AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT` + Entra credentials).
98. 
99. **Always wire the bundle, not the 4 separate evaluators:**
100. 
101. | Evaluator | Metrics produced | Notes |
102. |-----------|------------------|-------|
103. | `ContentHarmEvaluator` | `Hate And Unfairness`, `Self Harm`, `Violence`, `Sexual` | **Single-shot — one Foundry call returns all 4 metrics.** Always prefer this over the 4 separate evaluators below. |
104. 
105. Additional safety evaluators (each wired as separate `[TestMethod]`):
106. 
107. | Evaluator | Metric | Notes |
108. |-----------|--------|-------|
109. | `ProtectedMaterialEvaluator` | `Protected Material` | copyrighted material in output |
110. | `IndirectAttackEvaluator` | `Indirect Attack` | prompt-injection-style indirect attacks |
111. | `CodeVulnerabilityEvaluator` | `Code Vulnerability` | vulnerable code in output |
112. | `UngroundedAttributesEvaluator` | `Ungrounded Attributes` | inferred human attributes |
113. | `GroundednessProEvaluator` | `Groundedness Pro` | fine-tuned Foundry-hosted groundedness check |
114. 
115. The 4 separate evaluators (`HateAndUnfairnessEvaluator`,
116. `SelfHarmEvaluator`, `ViolenceEvaluator`, `SexualEvaluator`) are
117. **not** scaffolded — they're a strict subset of `ContentHarmEvaluator`
118. and cost 4× more Foundry calls for the same metrics.
119. 
120. ## Threshold mapping
121. 
122. `quality.thresholds.json` maps **real MEAI metric names** to minimum
123. `EvaluationRating` enum values:
124. 
125. ```json
126. {
127.   "schema_version": 2,
128.   "hard_fail": false,
129.   "thresholds": {
130.     "Relevance":   { "min_rating": "Good" },
131.     "Coherence":   { "min_rating": "Good" },
132.     "Fluency":     { "min_rating": "Average" },
133.     "Groundedness":{ "min_rating": "Good" },
134.     "BLEU":        { "min_value": 0.20 },
135.     "F1":          { "min_value": 0.30 },
136.     "Words":       { "min_value": 5, "max_value": 500 }
137.   }
138. }
139. ```
140. 
141. `hard_fail: true` makes any below-threshold metric fail the test.
142. Default `false` makes the test pass-through informational — failures
143. show in the report only.
144. 
145. ## Custom rubric-driven evaluator
146. 
147. The built-in Quality evaluators (Relevance, Coherence, Fluency,
148. Completeness, Equivalence) judge against generic rubrics baked into
149. the evaluator's judge prompt. They cannot read `Quality/rubric.md`.
150. That makes them ill-fitting for agents with deliberate stylistic
151. constraints (ELI5 / summarizer / strict-format / persona-bound
152. agents) — see `common-pitfalls.md#tuning-quality-for-stylistic-agents`.
153. 
154. For those agents, scaffold a `RubricEvaluator` that reads
155. `Quality/rubric.md` and asks the judge to score against *your*
156. criteria. The pattern is shape-identical to `WordCountEvaluator` —
157. it just delegates to the judge chat client.
158. 
159. ```csharp
160. // Reporting/RubricEvaluator.cs
161. // Custom rubric-driven evaluator. Reads Quality/rubric.md and asks
162. // the judge to score the response against per-app criteria. Emits a
163. // single "RubricFit" metric (numeric 1-5) plus a free-text rationale.
164. public sealed class RubricEvaluator : IEvaluator
165. {
166.     public const string MetricName = "RubricFit";
167.     public IReadOnlyCollection<string> EvaluationMetricNames { get; } = [MetricName];
168. 
169.     private readonly string _rubric;
170. 
171.     public RubricEvaluator(string rubricMarkdown) => _rubric = rubricMarkdown;
172. 
173.     public static RubricEvaluator FromFile(string path) =>
174.         new(File.ReadAllText(path));
175. 
176.     public async ValueTask<EvaluationResult> EvaluateAsync(
177.         IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
178.         ChatResponse modelResponse,
179.         ChatConfiguration? chatConfiguration = null,
180.         IEnumerable<EvaluationContext>? additionalContext = null,
181.         CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
182.     {
183.         if (chatConfiguration?.ChatClient is null)
184.         {
185.             // Judge tier not active — return a stubbed Inconclusive metric.
186.             return new EvaluationResult(new NumericMetric(MetricName)
187.             {
188.                 Interpretation = new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(
189.                     EvaluationRating.Inconclusive, reason: "Judge not wired.")
190.             });
191.         }
192. 
193.         var userQuery = string.Join("\n", messages.Select(m => m.Text));
194.         var responseText = modelResponse.Text ?? string.Empty;
195. 
196.         // NOTE: $$"""...""" (double-$) raw string. Inside, single { } is literal
197.         // (matters for the JSON braces below), and {{var}} is interpolation.
198.         // Plain $"""...""" would reject `{{ ... }}` as literal with CS9006.
199.         var prompt = $$"""
200.             You are scoring an assistant response against the rubric below.
201. 
202.             ## Rubric
203.             {{_rubric}}
204. 
205.             ## User query
206.             {{userQuery}}
207. 
208.             ## Assistant response
209.             {{responseText}}
210. 
211.             Respond with strict JSON: { "score": <1-5 int>, "rationale": "<1-2 sentences>" }.
212.             5 = perfectly satisfies every rubric clause. 1 = ignores the rubric.
213.             """;
214. 
215.         var judge = await chatConfiguration.ChatClient.GetResponseAsync(
216.             prompt, cancellationToken: cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
217. 
218.         // Tolerant parse: fall back to Inconclusive on bad JSON.
219.         var (score, rationale) = TryParse(judge.Text ?? "");
220. 
221.         var metric = new NumericMetric(MetricName, value: score)
222.         {
223.             Interpretation = new EvaluationMetricInterpretation(
224.                 rating: score switch { >= 4 => EvaluationRating.Good,
225.                                        3    => EvaluationRating.Average,
226.                                        _    => EvaluationRating.Poor },
227.                 reason: rationale)
228.         };
229.         return new EvaluationResult(metric);
230.     }
231. 
232.     private static (int score, string rationale) TryParse(string raw)
233.     {
234.         try
235.         {
236.             using var doc = JsonDocument.Parse(raw.Trim().Trim('`', ' ', '\n', '\r'));
237.             return (doc.RootElement.GetProperty("score").GetInt32(),
238.                     doc.RootElement.GetProperty("rationale").GetString() ?? "");
239.         }
240.         catch { return (3, "Judge response was unparseable; defaulted to Average."); }
241.     }
242. }
243. ```
244. 
245. Wire it from `Reporting/ReportingConfig.cs`'s judge-tier evaluator
246. list **alongside** Relevance/Coherence/Fluency (drop Completeness +
247. Equivalence per the pitfall guidance):
248. 
249. ```csharp
250. // In ReportingConfig.ForQuality(), when EvalEnv.UseRealJudge:
251. evaluators.Add(new RelevanceEvaluator());
252. evaluators.Add(new CoherenceEvaluator());
253. evaluators.Add(new FluencyEvaluator());
254. evaluators.Add(RubricEvaluator.FromFile(
255.     Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "Quality", "rubric.md")));
256. // CompletenessEvaluator + EquivalenceEvaluator deliberately dropped
257. // for this app — see common-pitfalls.md tuning section.
258. ```
259. 
260. Ensure `Quality/rubric.md` is copied to output by adding to the csproj:
261. 
262. ```xml
263. <ItemGroup>
264.   <None Update="Quality/rubric.md" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
265. </ItemGroup>
266. ```
267. 
268. This `RubricFit` metric will appear in `report.html` alongside the
269. built-ins, and the rationale shows in the per-scenario detail drawer.
270. Update `Reporting/MetricsGlossary.cs`'s `QualityEntries` constant to
271. add a one-line `RubricFit` definition pointing at `Quality/rubric.md`.

1. # Metrics glossary
2. 
3. Source of truth for the per-run `metrics-glossary.md` artifact that the
4. scaffolded `<App>.Evals.Tests/Reporting/MetricsGlossary.cs` writes next
5. to `report.html`. The aieval HTML report is data-bound JSON — it shows
6. numbers but no definitions — so we co-locate this glossary with the
7. report so a first-time reader has a one-page cheat-sheet.
8. 
9. The skill emits **only the entries for evaluators that actually ran** in
10. the active tier, so a stub-tier user sees Words/BLEU/GLEU/F1 and
11. nothing else.
12. 
13. ## NLP tier (deterministic, no LLM)
14. 
15. ### `Words`
16. - **Custom evaluator** scaffolded by this skill (see `evaluators-catalog.md`).
17. - **What it measures:** word count of the response text (whitespace-separated tokens, per `WordCountEvaluator`).
18. - **Scale:** integer ≥ 0.
19. - **Interpretation:** `< 5` → Poor (response too short / empty). `5–500` → Good. `> 500` → Average (response unusually long).
20. - **Trust for:** sanity-checking that the model produced *anything* and isn't running away with a 10-page essay.
21. - **Don't trust for:** quality. A 50-word wrong answer scores the same as a 50-word correct answer.
22. 
23. ### `BLEU` — Bilingual Evaluation Understudy
24. - **What it measures:** n-gram (1-4) overlap between the response and one or more reference strings, with a brevity penalty.
25. - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
26. - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.1 weak overlap, often paraphrased; ~0.1–0.3 normal for free-form generation; ~0.3–0.5 strong; > 0.5 near-quotation.
27. - **Trust for:** "is the response in the same lexical neighbourhood as the reference?" — useful as a regression signal when the reference is canonical.
28. - **Don't trust for:** semantic correctness. A correct paraphrase scores low; an incorrect copy-paste of reference fragments scores high.
29. - **Reference:** [`BLEUEvaluator` in MEAI.Evaluation.NLP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.bleuevaluator).
30. 
31. ### `GLEU` — Google-BLEU
32. - **What it measures:** sentence-level BLEU variant. Symmetric — penalises both missing reference n-grams and extra invented ones.
33. - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
34. - **Interpretation:** same buckets as BLEU; GLEU usually tracks BLEU but is less brittle on short outputs.
35. - **Trust for:** the same use cases as BLEU when individual scenarios are short (1-2 sentences) and BLEU's brevity penalty would be misleading.
36. - **Don't trust for:** any semantic claim. Same caveats as BLEU.
37. - **Reference:** [`GLEUEvaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.gleuevaluator).
38. 
39. ### `F1` — Token-level F1
40. - **What it measures:** harmonic mean of unigram precision and recall against the ground-truth string. Order-insensitive.
41. - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
42. - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.2 mostly-disjoint vocab; 0.3–0.5 typical for free-form generation; > 0.6 strong word-level match.
43. - **Trust for:** QA / extraction-style scenarios where the *set of words* matters more than phrasing (SQuAD-style benchmarks use this).
44. - **Don't trust for:** word-order-sensitive tasks (e.g., "yes" vs "no" answers buried in long output) — the F1 score will be high even if the polarity is wrong.
45. - **Reference:** [`F1Evaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.f1evaluator).
46. 
47. > **NLP-tier headline:** all three of BLEU/GLEU/F1 are *lexical* metrics.
48. > They're cheap, deterministic, and free, but they cannot tell you the
49. > response is *correct* — only that it's *similar in wording*. Treat them
50. > as a regression early-warning, not a quality verdict.
51. 
52. ## Quality tier (LLM-as-judge — `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE=1`)
53. 
54. All Quality metrics produce a 1-5 `EvaluationRating` (Poor → Excellent)
55. plus a free-text rationale from the judge model.
56. 
57. ### `Relevance`
58. - **What it measures:** does the response actually address the user's query?
59. - **Trust for:** catching off-topic regressions (model started monologuing about a different topic).
60. - **Don't trust for:** factual correctness — a *relevantly wrong* answer can score high.
61. 
62. ### `Coherence`
63. - **What it measures:** is the response logically structured / orderly / easy to follow?
64. - **Trust for:** detecting rambling, contradictory, or logically broken outputs.
65. - **Don't trust for:** depth or correctness — coherent nonsense scores high.
66. 
67. ### `Fluency`
68. - **What it measures:** grammar, readability, naturalness.
69. - **Trust for:** detecting broken-English / token-soup outputs from undertrained or quantised models.
70. - **Don't trust for:** anything beyond surface text quality. A fluent lie scores high.
71. 
72. ### `Completeness`
73. - **What it measures:** how comprehensive and accurate the response is, given a reference (`CompletenessEvaluatorContext(groundTruth)`).
74. - **Trust for:** catching responses that are correct but partial (covered 2 of 4 required points).
75. - **Don't trust for:** brevity-as-a-feature scenarios — a short-but-correct answer can score lower than a long-and-padded one.
76. 
77. ### `Equivalence`
78. - **What it measures:** semantic similarity between response and ground truth in the context of the original query.
79. - **Trust for:** distinguishing "right answer, different words" (high) from "wrong answer" (low). Better than BLEU/F1 when paraphrasing is acceptable.
80. - **Don't trust for:** any case where the ground truth is itself ambiguous or one of multiple valid answers.
81. 
82. ### `Groundedness`
83. - **What it measures:** alignment between the response and a supplied source-of-truth context (`GroundednessEvaluatorContext(context)`).
84. - **Trust for:** RAG pipelines — flags when the model invented facts not in the retrieved context.
85. - **Don't trust for:** open-ended chat without a context document.
86. 
87. ### Agentic-only
88. 
89. The skill wires these only when an `*.AppHost.csproj` is detected.
90. 
91. - **`Intent Resolution`** — did the model identify and resolve the user's actual intent (vs answering a related-but-different question)?
92. - **`Task Adherence`** — did the model stick to the assigned task or wander into other agent territory?
93. - **`Tool Call Accuracy`** — did the model invoke the right tools with the right arguments? Requires `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluatorContext`.
94. 
95. > **Quality-tier headline:** these are LLM-judge subjective scores. They
96. > drift across judge model versions. Pin the judge model in
97. > `quality.thresholds.json` if you want comparable scores across runs.
98. 
99. ## Safety tier (Foundry — `EVAL_USE_FOUNDRY_SAFETY=1`)
100. 
101. All Safety evaluators return a 1-5 severity (1 = safe, 5 = severe harm)
102. plus a confidence score. Each metric is an *output classifier* — it
103. inspects the model's response, not the input prompt.
104. 
105. ### `Hate And Unfairness`, `Self Harm`, `Violence`, `Sexual`
106. - Wired together as the single-shot `ContentHarmEvaluator` (one Foundry call → all 4 metrics).
107. - **Trust for:** detecting harmful content in agent outputs.
108. - **Don't trust for:** input-side filtering — these never see the user's prompt. Pair with input-side Azure AI Content Safety for full coverage.
109. 
110. ### `Protected Material`
111. - Detects copyrighted text / song lyrics / book passages reproduced in the output.
112. 
113. ### `Indirect Attack`
114. - Detects prompt-injection-style content that would indicate the model picked up an indirect attack from retrieved content or tool output. Closest thing to an input-side check available in this tier.
115. 
116. ### `Code Vulnerability`
117. - Flags vulnerable patterns in code the model emitted (SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, etc.).
118. 
119. ### `Ungrounded Attributes`
120. - Detects inferred human attributes (race, gender, age, religion, etc.) in the response that weren't in the input.
121. 
122. ### `Groundedness Pro`
123. - Foundry-hosted fine-tuned groundedness evaluator. More accurate than the open-source `GroundednessEvaluator` but costs a Foundry call per scenario.
124. 
125. > **Safety-tier headline:** all safety metrics are *output classifiers*.
126. > They protect downstream consumers from the agent's outputs; they do not
127. > protect the agent from its inputs.
128. 
129. ## Quick reference card
130. 
131. | Metric | Tier | Scale | Needs ground truth? | Needs LLM? |
132. |--------|------|-------|---------------------|-----------|
133. | Words | NLP | int | no | no |
134. | BLEU | NLP | 0-1 | yes (references) | no |
135. | GLEU | NLP | 0-1 | yes (references) | no |
136. | F1 | NLP | 0-1 | yes (one string) | no |
137. | Relevance / Coherence / Fluency | Quality | 1-5 | no | yes (judge) |
138. | Completeness / Equivalence | Quality | 1-5 | yes (one string) | yes (judge) |
139. | Groundedness | Quality | 1-5 | yes (context) | yes (judge) |
140. | Intent Resolution / Task Adherence | Quality (agentic) | 1-5 | no | yes (judge) |
141. | Tool Call Accuracy | Quality (agentic) | 1-5 | yes (expected_tool_calls) | yes (judge) |
142. | Content Harm bundle (4 metrics) | Safety | 1-5 severity | no | yes (Foundry) |
143. | Protected / Indirect / Code Vuln. / Ungrounded | Safety | 1-5 severity | varies | yes (Foundry) |
144. | Groundedness Pro | Safety | 1-5 | yes (context) | yes (Foundry) |
145.

 numbers but no definitions — so we co-locate this glossary with the
 report so a first-time reader has a one-page cheat-sheet.
 
 The skill emits **only the entries for evaluators that actually ran** in
 the active tier, so a stub-tier user sees Words/BLEU/GLEU/F1 and
 nothing else.
 
 ## NLP tier (deterministic, no LLM)
 
 ### `Words`
 - **Custom evaluator** scaffolded by this skill (see `evaluators-catalog.md`).
 - **What it measures:** word count of the response text (whitespace-separated tokens, per `WordCountEvaluator`).
 - **Scale:** integer ≥ 0.
 - **Interpretation:** `< 5` → Poor (response too short / empty). `5–500` → Good. `> 500` → Average (response unusually long).
 - **Trust for:** sanity-checking that the model produced *anything* and isn't running away with a 10-page essay.
 - **Don't trust for:** quality. A 50-word wrong answer scores the same as a 50-word correct answer.
 
 ### `BLEU` — Bilingual Evaluation Understudy
 - **What it measures:** n-gram (1-4) overlap between the response and one or more reference strings, with a brevity penalty.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.1 weak overlap, often paraphrased; ~0.1–0.3 normal for free-form generation; ~0.3–0.5 strong; > 0.5 near-quotation.
 - **Trust for:** "is the response in the same lexical neighbourhood as the reference?" — useful as a regression signal when the reference is canonical.
 - **Don't trust for:** semantic correctness. A correct paraphrase scores low; an incorrect copy-paste of reference fragments scores high.
 - **Reference:** [`BLEUEvaluator` in MEAI.Evaluation.NLP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.bleuevaluator).
 
 ### `GLEU` — Google-BLEU
 - **What it measures:** sentence-level BLEU variant. Symmetric — penalises both missing reference n-grams and extra invented ones.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** same buckets as BLEU; GLEU usually tracks BLEU but is less brittle on short outputs.
 - **Trust for:** the same use cases as BLEU when individual scenarios are short (1-2 sentences) and BLEU's brevity penalty would be misleading.
 - **Don't trust for:** any semantic claim. Same caveats as BLEU.
 - **Reference:** [`GLEUEvaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.gleuevaluator).
 
 ### `F1` — Token-level F1
 - **What it measures:** harmonic mean of unigram precision and recall against the ground-truth string. Order-insensitive.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.2 mostly-disjoint vocab; 0.3–0.5 typical for free-form generation; > 0.6 strong word-level match.
 - **Trust for:** QA / extraction-style scenarios where the *set of words* matters more than phrasing (SQuAD-style benchmarks use this).
 - **Don't trust for:** word-order-sensitive tasks (e.g., "yes" vs "no" answers buried in long output) — the F1 score will be high even if the polarity is wrong.
 - **Reference:** [`F1Evaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.f1evaluator).
 
 > **NLP-tier headline:** all three of BLEU/GLEU/F1 are *lexical* metrics.
 > They're cheap, deterministic, and free, but they cannot tell you the
 > response is *correct* — only that it's *similar in wording*. Treat them
 > as a regression early-warning, not a quality verdict.
 
 ## Quality tier (LLM-as-judge — `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE=1`)
 
 All Quality metrics produce a 1-5 `EvaluationRating` (Poor → Excellent)
 plus a free-text rationale from the judge model.
 
 ### `Relevance`
 - **What it measures:** does the response actually address the user's query?
 - **Trust for:** catching off-topic regressions (model started monologuing about a different topic).
 - **Don't trust for:** factual correctness — a *relevantly wrong* answer can score high.
 
 ### `Coherence`
 - **What it measures:** is the response logically structured / orderly / easy to follow?
 - **Trust for:** detecting rambling, contradictory, or logically broken outputs.
 - **Don't trust for:** depth or correctness — coherent nonsense scores high.
 
 ### `Fluency`
 - **What it measures:** grammar, readability, naturalness.
 - **Trust for:** detecting broken-English / token-soup outputs from undertrained or quantised models.
 - **Don't trust for:** anything beyond surface text quality. A fluent lie scores high.
 
 ### `Completeness`
 - **What it measures:** how comprehensive and accurate the response is, given a reference (`CompletenessEvaluatorContext(groundTruth)`).
 - **Trust for:** catching responses that are correct but partial (covered 2 of 4 required points).
 - **Don't trust for:** brevity-as-a-feature scenarios — a short-but-correct answer can score lower than a long-and-padded one.
 
 ### `Equivalence`
 - **What it measures:** semantic similarity between response and ground truth in the context of the original query.
 - **Trust for:** distinguishing "right answer, different words" (high) from "wrong answer" (low). Better than BLEU/F1 when paraphrasing is acceptable.
 - **Don't trust for:** any case where the ground truth is itself ambiguous or one of multiple valid answers.
 
 ### `Groundedness`
 - **What it measures:** alignment between the response and a supplied source-of-truth context (`GroundednessEvaluatorContext(context)`).
 - **Trust for:** RAG pipelines — flags when the model invented facts not in the retrieved context.
 - **Don't trust for:** open-ended chat without a context document.
 
 ### Agentic-only
 
 The skill wires these only when an `*.AppHost.csproj` is detected.
 
 - **`Intent Resolution`** — did the model identify and resolve the user's actual intent (vs answering a related-but-different question)?
 - **`Task Adherence`** — did the model stick to the assigned task or wander into other agent territory?
 - **`Tool Call Accuracy`** — did the model invoke the right tools with the right arguments? Requires `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluatorContext`.
 
 > **Quality-tier headline:** these are LLM-judge subjective scores. They
 > drift across judge model versions. Pin the judge model in
 > `quality.thresholds.json` if you want comparable scores across runs.
 
 ## Safety tier (Foundry — `EVAL_USE_FOUNDRY_SAFETY=1`)
 
 All Safety evaluators return a 1-5 severity (1 = safe, 5 = severe harm)
 plus a confidence score. Each metric is an *output classifier* — it
 inspects the model's response, not the input prompt.
 
 ### `Hate And Unfairness`, `Self Harm`, `Violence`, `Sexual`
 - Wired together as the single-shot `ContentHarmEvaluator` (one Foundry call → all 4 metrics).
 - **Trust for:** detecting harmful content in agent outputs.
 - **Don't trust for:** input-side filtering — these never see the user's prompt. Pair with input-side Azure AI Content Safety for full coverage.
 
 ### `Protected Material`
 - Detects copyrighted text / song lyrics / book passages reproduced in the output.
 
 ### `Indirect Attack`
 - Detects prompt-injection-style content that would indicate the model picked up an indirect attack from retrieved content or tool output. Closest thing to an input-side check available in this tier.
 
 ### `Code Vulnerability`
 - Flags vulnerable patterns in code the model emitted (SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, etc.).
 
 ### `Ungrounded Attributes`
 - Detects inferred human attributes (race, gender, age, religion, etc.) in the response that weren't in the input.
 
 ### `Groundedness Pro`
 - Foundry-hosted fine-tuned groundedness evaluator. More accurate than the open-source `GroundednessEvaluator` but costs a Foundry call per scenario.
 
 > **Safety-tier headline:** all safety metrics are *output classifiers*.
 > They protect downstream consumers from the agent's outputs; they do not
 > protect the agent from its inputs.

 # Metrics glossary
 
 Source of truth for the per-run `metrics-glossary.md` artifact that the
 scaffolded `<App>.Evals.Tests/Reporting/MetricsGlossary.cs` writes next
 to `report.html`. The aieval HTML report is data-bound JSON — it shows
 numbers but no definitions — so we co-locate this glossary with the
 report so a first-time reader has a one-page cheat-sheet.
 
 The skill emits **only the entries for evaluators that actually ran** in
 the active tier, so a stub-tier user sees Words/BLEU/GLEU/F1 and
 nothing else.
 
 ## NLP tier (deterministic, no LLM)
 
 ### `Words`
 - **Custom evaluator** scaffolded by this skill (see `evaluators-catalog.md`).
 - **What it measures:** word count of the response text (whitespace-separated tokens, per `WordCountEvaluator`).
 - **Scale:** integer ≥ 0.
 - **Interpretation:** `< 5` → Poor (response too short / empty). `5–500` → Good. `> 500` → Average (response unusually long).
 - **Trust for:** sanity-checking that the model produced *anything* and isn't running away with a 10-page essay.
 - **Don't trust for:** quality. A 50-word wrong answer scores the same as a 50-word correct answer.
 
 ### `BLEU` — Bilingual Evaluation Understudy
 - **What it measures:** n-gram (1-4) overlap between the response and one or more reference strings, with a brevity penalty.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.1 weak overlap, often paraphrased; ~0.1–0.3 normal for free-form generation; ~0.3–0.5 strong; > 0.5 near-quotation.
 - **Trust for:** "is the response in the same lexical neighbourhood as the reference?" — useful as a regression signal when the reference is canonical.
 - **Don't trust for:** semantic correctness. A correct paraphrase scores low; an incorrect copy-paste of reference fragments scores high.
 - **Reference:** [`BLEUEvaluator` in MEAI.Evaluation.NLP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.bleuevaluator).
 
 ### `GLEU` — Google-BLEU
 - **What it measures:** sentence-level BLEU variant. Symmetric — penalises both missing reference n-grams and extra invented ones.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** same buckets as BLEU; GLEU usually tracks BLEU but is less brittle on short outputs.
 - **Trust for:** the same use cases as BLEU when individual scenarios are short (1-2 sentences) and BLEU's brevity penalty would be misleading.
 - **Don't trust for:** any semantic claim. Same caveats as BLEU.
 - **Reference:** [`GLEUEvaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.gleuevaluator).
 
 ### `F1` — Token-level F1
 - **What it measures:** harmonic mean of unigram precision and recall against the ground-truth string. Order-insensitive.
 - **Scale:** 0.0 – 1.0.
 - **Interpretation:** ~0.0–0.2 mostly-disjoint vocab; 0.3–0.5 typical for free-form generation; > 0.6 strong word-level match.
 - **Trust for:** QA / extraction-style scenarios where the *set of words* matters more than phrasing (SQuAD-style benchmarks use this).
 - **Don't trust for:** word-order-sensitive tasks (e.g., "yes" vs "no" answers buried in long output) — the F1 score will be high even if the polarity is wrong.
 - **Reference:** [`F1Evaluator`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.nlp.f1evaluator).
 
 > **NLP-tier headline:** all three of BLEU/GLEU/F1 are *lexical* metrics.
 > They're cheap, deterministic, and free, but they cannot tell you the
 > response is *correct* — only that it's *similar in wording*. Treat them
 > as a regression early-warning, not a quality verdict.
 
 ## Quality tier (LLM-as-judge — `EVAL_USE_REAL_JUDGE=1`)
 
 All Quality metrics produce a 1-5 `EvaluationRating` (Poor → Excellent)
 plus a free-text rationale from the judge model.
 
 ### `Relevance`
 - **What it measures:** does the response actually address the user's query?
 - **Trust for:** catching off-topic regressions (model started monologuing about a different topic).
 - **Don't trust for:** factual correctness — a *relevantly wrong* answer can score high.
 
 ### `Coherence`
 - **What it measures:** is the response logically structured / orderly / easy to follow?
 - **Trust for:** detecting rambling, contradictory, or logically broken outputs.
 - **Don't trust for:** depth or correctness — coherent nonsense scores high.
 
 ### `Fluency`
 - **What it measures:** grammar, readability, naturalness.
 - **Trust for:** detecting broken-English / token-soup outputs from undertrained or quantised models.
 - **Don't trust for:** anything beyond surface text quality. A fluent lie scores high.
 
 ### `Completeness`
 - **What it measures:** how comprehensive and accurate the response is, given a reference (`CompletenessEvaluatorContext(groundTruth)`).
 - **Trust for:** catching responses that are correct but partial (covered 2 of 4 required points).
 - **Don't trust for:** brevity-as-a-feature scenarios — a short-but-correct answer can score lower than a long-and-padded one.
 
 ### `Equivalence`
 - **What it measures:** semantic similarity between response and ground truth in the context of the original query.
 - **Trust for:** distinguishing "right answer, different words" (high) from "wrong answer" (low). Better than BLEU/F1 when paraphrasing is acceptable.
 - **Don't trust for:** any case where the ground truth is itself ambiguous or one of multiple valid answers.
 
 ### `Groundedness`
 - **What it measures:** alignment between the response and a supplied source-of-truth context (`GroundednessEvaluatorContext(context)`).
 - **Trust for:** RAG pipelines — flags when the model invented facts not in the retrieved context.
 - **Don't trust for:** open-ended chat without a context document.
 
 ### Agentic-only
 
 The skill wires these only when an `*.AppHost.csproj` is detected.
 
 - **`Intent Resolution`** — did the model identify and resolve the user's actual intent (vs answering a related-but-different question)?
 - **`Task Adherence`** — did the model stick to the assigned task or wander into other agent territory?
 - **`Tool Call Accuracy`** — did the model invoke the right tools with the right arguments? Requires `ToolCallAccuracyEvaluatorContext`.
 
 > **Quality-tier headline:** these are LLM-judge subjective scores. They
 > drift across judge model versions. Pin the judge model in
 > `quality.thresholds.json` if you want comparable scores across runs.
 
 ## Safety tier (Foundry — `EVAL_USE_FOUNDRY_SAFETY=1`)
 
 All Safety evaluators return a 1-5 severity (1 = safe, 5 = severe harm)
 plus a confidence score. Each metric is an *output classifier* — it
 inspects the model's response, not the input prompt.
 
 ### `Hate And Unfairness`, `Self Harm`, `Violence`, `Sexual`
 - Wired together as the single-shot `ContentHarmEvaluator` (one Foundry call → all 4 metrics).
 - **Trust for:** detecting harmful content in agent outputs.
 - **Don't trust for:** input-side filtering — these never see the user's prompt. Pair with input-side Azure AI Content Safety for full coverage.
 
 ### `Protected Material`
 - Detects copyrighted text / song lyrics / book passages reproduced in the output.
 
 ### `Indirect Attack`
 - Detects prompt-injection-style content that would indicate the model picked up an indirect attack from retrieved content or tool output. Closest thing to an input-side check available in this tier.
 
 ### `Code Vulnerability`
 - Flags vulnerable patterns in code the model emitted (SQL injection, hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, etc.).
 
 ### `Ungrounded Attributes`
 - Detects inferred human attributes (race, gender, age, religion, etc.) in the response that weren't in the input.
 
 ### `Groundedness Pro`
 - Foundry-hosted fine-tuned groundedness evaluator. More accurate than the open-source `GroundednessEvaluator` but costs a Foundry call per scenario.
 
 > **Safety-tier headline:** all safety metrics are *output classifiers*.
 > They protect downstream consumers from the agent's outputs; they do not
 > protect the agent from its inputs.
 
 ## Quick reference card
 
 | Metric | Tier | Scale | Needs ground truth? | Needs LLM? |
 |--------|------|-------|---------------------|-----------|
 | Words | NLP | int | no | no |
 | BLEU | NLP | 0-1 | yes (references) | no |
 | GLEU | NLP | 0-1 | yes (references) | no |
 | F1 | NLP | 0-1 | yes (one string) | no |
 | Relevance / Coherence / Fluency | Quality | 1-5 | no | yes (judge) |
 | Completeness / Equivalence | Quality | 1-5 | yes (one string) | yes (judge) |
 | Groundedness | Quality | 1-5 | yes (context) | yes (judge) |
 | Intent Resolution / Task Adherence | Quality (agentic) | 1-5 | no | yes (judge) |
 | Tool Call Accuracy | Quality (agentic) | 1-5 | yes (expected_tool_calls) | yes (judge) |
 | Content Harm bundle (4 metrics) | Safety | 1-5 severity | no | yes (Foundry) |
 | Protected / Indirect / Code Vuln. / Ungrounded | Safety | 1-5 severity | varies | yes (Foundry) |
 | Groundedness Pro | Safety | 1-5 | yes (context) | yes (Foundry) |
 
 ## `MetricsGlossary.cs` template
 
 The scaffolded `<App>.Evals.Tests/Reporting/MetricsGlossary.cs` writes
 the tier-relevant slice of this glossary next to `report.html` after
 each `dotnet test` run.
 
 > **MSTest constraint:** an assembly may declare **only one**
 > `[AssemblyCleanup]` method. The skill emits `MetricsGlossary` as a
 > plain static class (no `[TestClass]`, no `[AssemblyCleanup]`) and
 > chains `MetricsGlossary.WriteGlossary()` from
 > `AievalReport.GenerateReport`'s single `[AssemblyCleanup]`.
 > Wrap the call in a `try/catch` so a glossary-write failure never
 > masks the report.
 
 ```csharp
 internal static class MetricsGlossary
 {
     public static void WriteGlossary()
     {
         var outDir = Path.Combine(
             RepoRoot.Find(), ".copilot", "perf-reports", "evals", EvalEnv.ReportFolder);
         Directory.CreateDirectory(outDir);
         var path = Path.Combine(outDir, "metrics-glossary.md");
 
         var sb = new StringBuilder();
         sb.AppendLine($"# Metrics glossary — {EvalEnv.Tier} tier");
         sb.AppendLine();
         sb.AppendLine($"Generated: {DateTime.UtcNow:O}");
         sb.AppendLine();
         sb.AppendLine($"Companion to `report.html` in this folder. The aieval HTML report shows numbers; this file explains them.");
         sb.AppendLine();
 
         sb.AppendLine(NlpEntries);
         if (EvalEnv.UseRealJudge) sb.AppendLine(QualityEntries);
         if (EvalEnv.UseFoundrySafety) sb.AppendLine(SafetyEntries);
 
         sb.AppendLine();
         sb.AppendLine("> Source: setup-maf-evals references/metrics-glossary.md");
 
         File.WriteAllText(path, sb.ToString());
         Console.WriteLine($"[MetricsGlossary] {path}");
     }
 
     private const string NlpEntries = """
         ## NLP tier (deterministic, no LLM)
         - **Words** (int): response length sanity check. <5 too short, 5-500 ok, >500 long.
         - **BLEU** (0-1): n-gram overlap with reference(s). 0.1-0.3 normal, >0.3 strong, >0.5 near-quotation. *Lexical, not semantic.*
         - **GLEU** (0-1): sentence-level BLEU; better for short outputs. Same buckets as BLEU.
         - **F1** (0-1): unigram token F1 vs ground-truth. 0.3-0.5 typical, >0.6 strong word-level match. Order-insensitive.
 
         > Headline: NLP metrics measure wording similarity, not correctness. Use for regression early-warning, not as quality verdicts.
         """;
 
     private const string QualityEntries = """
         ## Quality tier (LLM-as-judge)
         Each rated 1-5 (Poor → Excellent) with a free-text rationale.
         - **Relevance**: addresses the user's query. Catches off-topic regressions.
         - **Coherence**: logically structured. Catches rambling/contradictory outputs.
         - **Fluency**: grammar/readability. Catches broken-English outputs.
         - **Completeness** (needs reference): comprehensive and accurate.
         - **Equivalence** (needs reference): semantic similarity in context of the query.
         - **Groundedness** (needs context): aligned with supplied source-of-truth.
         - **Intent Resolution / Task Adherence / Tool Call Accuracy** (agentic only).
 
         > Headline: judge scores drift across model versions. Pin the judge model for comparable runs.
         """;
 
     private const string SafetyEntries = """
         ## Safety tier (Foundry)
         Each rated 1-5 severity (1 safe → 5 severe).
         - **ContentHarm bundle** (single-shot, 4 metrics): Hate-And-Unfairness, Self-Harm, Violence, Sexual.
         - **Protected Material**: copyrighted text reproduced.
         - **Indirect Attack**: prompt-injection content from retrieved/tool data.
         - **Code Vulnerability**: vulnerable code patterns (SQLi, weak crypto, etc.).
         - **Ungrounded Attributes**: inferred human attributes not in input.
         - **Groundedness Pro**: Foundry-hosted fine-tuned groundedness check.
 
         > Headline: all safety metrics inspect *outputs*, not inputs. Pair with Azure AI Content Safety on the request side for full coverage.
         """;
 }
 ```

 {

         catch (Exception ex) { Console.Error.WriteLine($"[MetricsGlossary] Failed: {ex.Message}"); }

 # `dotnet-tools.json` manifest
 
 The skill scaffolds a **local** tool manifest. Global install is
 explicitly avoided — pinning the tool version to the project makes
 evals reproducible across machines and CI runs.
 
 ## Why local
 
 - Reproducible: every clone gets the exact same `aieval` version.
 - CI-friendly: `dotnet tool restore` in the workflow is one line.
 - No PATH conflicts with developers who may have other versions installed.
 
 ## Generation (do not hand-write the version)
 
 Generate the manifest instead of authoring a pinned version literal:
 
 ```pwsh
 cd <App>.Evals.Tests
 dotnet new tool-manifest                                          # if none exists
 dotnet tool install microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.console    # latest; provides `aieval`
 ```
 
 `dotnet tool install` (no `--version`) records the **current** tool version into
 the manifest and defaults to `rollForward: false`, so you still get a pinned,
 reproducible entry — but NuGet chose the number, not the skill. The resulting
 manifest looks like this (version shown is an illustrative snapshot):
 
 ```json
 {
   "version": 1,
   "isRoot": true,
   "tools": {
     "microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.console": {
       "version": "10.7.0",
       "commands": ["aieval"],
       "rollForward": false
     }
   }
 }
 ```
 
 `dotnet new tool-manifest` places the file per the SDK default — conventionally
 `<App>.Evals.Tests/.config/dotnet-tools.json`, though newer SDKs may write a
 repo-root-style `dotnet-tools.json` in the current directory. Either way, run
 `dotnet tool restore` / `dotnet tool run` **from the `<App>.Evals.Tests/`
 directory** so discovery finds the manifest. Running them from the repo root
 would walk *up* and could miss a manifest that lives in a child directory, so the
 CI `Restore tools` step, the `aieval report` safety-net step, and the runtime
 `AssemblyCleanup` report call all use the test-project directory as their working
 directory. The skill emits `dotnet tool restore` as the next step in the chat
 output after scaffolding.
 
 ## Why `rollForward: false`
 
 The output of `aieval report` is consumed by humans visually and by
 artifact comparison in CI. A silent rollForward of the tool to a
 newer version can change report layout, charts, or metric grouping —
 breaking trend comparisons and visual diffs.
 
 If a user wants to upgrade the tool, the skill should emit a
 `dotnet tool update microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.console`
 command in the chat output (with a note: "this may change report
 layout").
 
 ## Conflict with existing manifest
 
 If `dotnet-tools.json` already exists at the project (or any parent
 directory), the skill **merges** the `aieval` entry rather than
 overwriting. If a different version of `aieval` is already pinned,
 surface the diff in chat output and require user confirmation.

 would walk *up* and could miss a manifest that lives in a child directory, so the
 CI `Restore tools` step, the `aieval report` safety-net step, and the runtime
 `AssemblyCleanup` report call all use the test-project directory as their working
 directory. The skill emits `dotnet tool restore` as the next step in the chat
 output after scaffolding.
 
 ## Why `rollForward: false`
 
 The output of `aieval report` is consumed by humans visually and by
 artifact comparison in CI. A silent rollForward of the tool to a
 newer version can change report layout, charts, or metric grouping —
 breaking trend comparisons and visual diffs.
 
 If a user wants to upgrade the tool, the skill should emit a
 `dotnet tool update microsoft.extensions.ai.evaluation.console`
 command in the chat output (with a note: "this may change report
 layout").
 
 ## Conflict with existing manifest
 
 If `dotnet-tools.json` already exists at the project (or any parent
 directory), the skill **merges** the `aieval` entry rather than
 overwriting. If a different version of `aieval` is already pinned,
 surface the diff in chat output and require user confirmation.
